public_rationale: METR's July 2025 study found that experienced open-source developers took 19% longer to finish tasks when allowed to use AI tools. Beforehand, they expected AI to speed them up by 24%. So Zitron's report of the study's numbers is accurate. One small point: 24% was the speedup they expected before starting. After the tasks, they believed AI had sped them up by 20%. The gap between belief and result still holds either way. The study covered 16 experienced open-source developers using early-2025 tools, not engineers in general. In February 2026, METR said it believes developers are probably sped up more by current tools, and it later marked the 2025 results as out of date. That is context, not a correction of what the 2025 study said.
limitations: '24% faster' blends the developers' 24% expectation before the tasks with the 20% speedup they believed in afterwards.
The study had a small, specific sample, and METR warns against generalizing it to all engineers or to later tools.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: LLM coding tools made engineers 19% slower despite their belief they were 24% faster, per a 2025 METR study.

statement.excerpt: A study from last year from METR said that despite thinking they were 24% faster, LLM coding tools made engineers 19% slower.

from_speaker: a study from last year from METR
LLM coding tools made engineers 19% slower
our_interpretation: The claim reports what a 2025 METR study found. It is supported if that study found developers took about 19% longer with AI tools while believing AI would speed them up by about 24%.
'Engineers' is read as the study's participants (experienced open-source developers), not all engineers. His sentence states the study's result, not a general law.
'Thinking they were 24% faster' is read as the developers' 24% expected speedup. The study separately reports a 20% speedup they believed in after the tasks.
criteria.support_condition: METR's 2025 study reports a slowdown of about 19% with AI tools, together with a perceived or expected speedup of about 24%.
criteria.contradiction_condition: METR's 2025 study reports a materially different slowdown, a speedup, or no gap between perceived and measured effect.

evidence.excerpt: When developers are allowed to use AI tools, they take 19% longer to complete issues—a significant slowdown that goes against developer beliefs and expert forecasts. This gap between perception and reality is striking: developers expected AI to speed them up by 24%, and even after experiencing the slowdown, they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%.
